modules.summary: This module develops the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and turns it into two working tools for positive integers: computing the HCF and LCM of two or three numbers, and verifying the product identity HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b. Starting from the observation that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way, it introduces the factor-tree and prime-factorisation methods as the everyday interface to the theorem. Segment S1 states Theorem 1.1 and uses its uniqueness clause to argue that 4ⁿ can never end in the digit zero. Segment S2 converts Theorem 1.1 into the HCF rule "product of the smallest power of each common prime factor", while Segment S3 derives the twin LCM rule "product of the greatest power of each prime factor involved" and the two-number identity. Segment S4 extends both rules to three numbers, shows that HCF(a,b,c) × LCM(a,b,c) ≠ a × b × c, and consolidates the toolkit through the Exercise 1.1 word problems on tiling, jogging, and divisibility. The unifying insight throughout is that the prime-power representation of every positive integer, guaranteed by Theorem 1.1, is what makes HCF, LCM and divisibility arguments mechanical. This prepares the ground for Module 2, where the same theorem is used to prove that √2, √3 and √5 are irrational.

topics.summary: This opening topic previews the two central results of Chapter 1 and explains why prime numbers are the atoms of the positive integers. Euclid's division algorithm is the familiar long-division fact that any positive integer a, when divided by a positive integer b, leaves a remainder r smaller than b; it is the chapter's main tool for computing HCFs. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number factorises into primes uniquely, and it is used later in the chapter both to compute HCF and LCM and to prove that √2, √3 and √5 are irrational. For example, 253 = 11 × 23 and 4 = 2 × 2 show the "build-up" direction, while any number can also be decomposed downward into primes. Students use this orientation whenever they meet a problem about divisibility, factorisation, or irrationality in the rest of the chapter.
topics.topic_name: Chapter Introduction: Building Numbers from Primes
topics.brief_summary: The chapter introduces Euclid's division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic as the two central properties of positive integers, used to compute HCF and to prove irrationality.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: In Class IX, you met irrational numbers for the first time and placed a few of them on the real number line. This chapter takes that story further by returning to the positive integers with a simple question. What are the building blocks of every natural number, and what can those blocks tell us about numbers that are not whole?

RECALL: You already know that a prime number has exactly two factors, namely 1 and itself, while a composite number has more than two factors.

CORE: Section 1.2 focuses on two very important properties of positive integers. The first is Euclid's division algorithm. Stated simply, it says that any positive integer a can be divided by another positive integer b so that it leaves a remainder r smaller than b. Many of you probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although the result is straightforward to state, it has many applications related to the divisibility properties of integers, and we will use it mainly to compute the HCF of two positive integers.

The second property is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. This theorem has to do with the multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way, and that one sentence is essentially the whole theorem. Easy to state, yet it has very deep applications. We will use it for two main purposes in this chapter. First, we will prove the irrationality of numbers such as √2, √3 and √5, numbers you only accepted as irrational in Class IX. Second, we will apply it to determine exactly when the decimal expansion of a rational number p/q (q ≠ 0) terminates and when it is non-terminating repeating. The prime factorisation of the denominator q will completely reveal the nature of the decimal expansion of p/q.

MULTIPLYING PRIMES TO BUILD NUMBERS: In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a product of its prime factors. For instance, 2 = 2, 4 = 2 × 2, and 253 = 11 × 23, and so on. Now let us look at natural numbers from the other direction. Can any natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers together in some combination? That question is the door into this chapter.

ERROR ALERT: Many students initially think primes are rare curiosities used only for factor-tree exercises. In reality, primes are the atoms of the positive integers: every composite number is assembled from them.

CHECK: In one sentence, how would you explain to a Class IX student why Euclid's division algorithm is really just the long-division procedure they already use?
topics.original_chunk:
1.1 Introduction

In Class IX, you began your exploration of the world of real numbers and encountered irrational numbers. We continue our discussion on real numbers in this chapter. We begin with very important properties of positive integers in Sections 1.2, namely the Euclid's division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

Euclid's division algorithm, as the name suggests, has to do with divisibility of integers. Stated simply, it says any positive integer a can be divided by another positive integer b in such a way that it leaves a remainder r that is smaller than b. Many of you probably recognise this as the usual long division process. Although this result is quite easy to state and understand, it has many applications related to the divisibility properties of integers. We touch upon a few of them, and use it mainly to compute the HCF of two positive integers.

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, on the other hand, has to do something with multiplication of positive integers. You already know that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way — this important fact is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Again, while it is a result that is easy to state and understand, it has some very deep and significant applications in the field of mathematics. We use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic for two main applications. First, we use it to prove the irrationality of many of the numbers you studied in Class IX, such as √2, √3 and √5. Second, we apply this theorem to explore when exactly the decimal expansion of a rational number, say p/q (q ≠ 0), is terminating and when it is non-terminating repeating. We do so by looking at the prime factorisation of the denominator q of p/q. You will see that the prime factorisation of q will completely reveal the nature of the decimal expansion of p/q.

So let us begin our exploration.

1.2 The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

In your earlier classes, you have seen that any natural number can be written as a product of its prime factors. For instance, 2 = 2, 4 = 2 × 2, 253 = 11 × 23, and so on. Now, let us try and look at natural numbers from the other direction. That is, can any natural number be obtained by multiplying prime numbers? Let us see.
concept_bullets: Euclid's division algorithm is just the usual long-division fact — for example, dividing 17 by 5 gives quotient 3 and remainder 2, with 2 < 5.
Every composite number is built from primes by multiplication — for example, 253 = 11 × 23 and 4 = 2 × 2, combining primes from a small pantry.
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic is later used to prove that numbers such as √2, √3 and √5 are irrational.
The prime factorisation of the denominator q tells us whether the decimal expansion of p/q terminates or is non-terminating repeating.

recall_questions.answer: (1) Euclid's division algorithm: any positive integer a can be divided by another positive integer b so that it leaves a remainder r smaller than b. (2) Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way, apart from the order of the factors.
recall_questions.prompt: State, in one sentence each, the two central results the chapter introduces in Section 1.2.

recall_questions.answer: In the build-up direction, we start with primes and multiply them in different combinations to produce natural numbers (e.g., 2 x 2 = 4, 11 x 23 = 253). In the factor-tree direction, we start with a composite number and keep splitting it until only primes remain. Both directions show that every natural number is built from primes, so primes are the atoms of the positive integers.
recall_questions.prompt: Explain why prime numbers are called the 'building blocks' of every natural number. Use the build-up and factor-tree directions in your answer.

recall_questions.answer: Application 1: Proving that numbers such as √(2), √(3) and √(5) are irrational, instead of only accepting this fact from Class IX. Application 2: Determining when the decimal expansion of a rational number p/q (q not equal to 0) terminates and when it is non-terminating repeating, by examining the prime factorisation of the denominator q.
recall_questions.prompt: The chapter states the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic has two main applications. Name them and give one sentence describing each.

topics.summary: Theorem 1.1, the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, states that every composite number can be factorised as a product of primes, and that this factorisation is unique apart from the order of the prime factors. The method is the factor tree: pick any prime that divides the number cleanly, split, and repeat on each composite branch until only primes remain. For example, the factor tree for 32760 — 32760 → 2 × 16380 → 2 × 8190 → 2 × 4095 → 3 × 1365 → 3 × 455 → 5 × 91 → 7 × 13 — gives 32760 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13 in prime-power form. Writing primes in ascending order makes this representation unique, which is the reason the theorem supports every later HCF, LCM and irrationality argument in the chapter.
topics.topic_name: Statement of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
topics.brief_summary: Theorem 1.1 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) states that every composite number factorises as a product of primes uniquely apart from order, illustrated by 32760 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Take any small collection of primes and multiply them in different combinations. Can you reach every composite number you can think of, or will some remain out of reach? This topic answers that question decisively.

RECALL: From the previous topic, we want to look at natural numbers from the build-up direction: starting with primes and multiplying them to produce larger numbers.

CORE — Building numbers from primes: Take any collection of prime numbers, say 2, 3, 7, 11 and 23. If we multiply some or all of these numbers, allowing them to repeat as many times as we wish, we can produce a large collection of positive integers. In fact, we can produce infinitely many. Let us list a few:

7 × 11 × 23 = 1771
3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 5313
2 × 3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 10626
2³ × 3 × 7³ = 8232
2² × 3 × 7 × 11 × 23 = 21252

and so on.

Now suppose your collection of primes includes all the possible primes. What is your guess about the size of this collection? Does it contain only a finite number of integers, or infinitely many? In fact, there are infinitely many primes. So, if we combine all these primes in all possible ways, we will get an infinite collection of numbers: all the primes and all possible products of primes. The natural question is — can we produce all the composite numbers this way? Do you think there may be a composite number which is not the product of powers of primes?

FACTORISING IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: Before answering, let us factorise positive integers; that is, do the opposite of what we have done so far. We will use the factor tree with which you are familiar. Consider the large number 32760 and factorise it step by step:

32760 → 2 × 16380 → 2 × 8190 → 2 × 4095 → 3 × 1365 → 3 × 455 → 5 × 91 → 7 × 13

So we have factorised 32760 as 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 13, i.e., 32760 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13 as a product of powers of primes.

WHY THIS STEP? We kept dividing by the smallest prime that divides cleanly. Why? Because it guarantees we end only when every remaining factor is prime, so the tree terminates and gives us an honest prime factorisation.

Let us try another number, say 123456789. This can be written as 3² × 3803 × 3607. Of course, you have to check that 3803 and 3607 are primes. (Try it out for several other natural numbers yourself.) This leads us to a conjecture that every composite number can be written as the product of powers of primes. In fact, this statement is true, and it is called the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic because of its basic, crucial importance to the study of integers. Let us now formally state this theorem.

Theorem 1.1 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic): Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

HISTORICAL NOTE: An equivalent version of Theorem 1.1 was probably first recorded as Proposition 14 of Book IX in Euclid's Elements, before it came to be known as the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. However, the first correct proof was given by Carl Friedrich Gauss in his Disquisitiones Arithmeticae. Carl Friedrich Gauss is often referred to as the 'Prince of Mathematicians' and is considered one of the three greatest mathematicians of all time, along with Archimedes and Newton. He has made fundamental contributions to both mathematics and science.

UNPACKING THE WORD "UNIQUE": The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every composite number can be factorised as a product of primes. Actually it says more. It says that given any composite number, it can be factorised as a product of prime numbers in a unique way, except for the order in which the primes occur. That is, given any composite number there is one and only one way to write it as a product of primes, as long as we are not particular about the order in which the primes are written. So, for example, we regard 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 as the same as 3 × 5 × 7 × 2, or any other possible order in which these primes are written. This fact is also stated in the following form:

The prime factorisation of a natural number is unique, except for the order of its factors.

GENERAL FORM: Given a composite number x, we factorise it as x = p₁p₂…pₙ, where p₁, p₂, …, pₙ are primes written in ascending order, i.e., p₁ ≤ p₂ ≤ … ≤ pₙ. If we combine the same primes, we get powers of primes. For example, 32760 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 13 = 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13.

WHY THIS STEP? We agreed to write the primes in ascending order. Why? Because once the order is fixed, the factorisation is determined completely; there is no room for two different-looking prime lists to describe the same number.

Once we have decided that the order will be ascending, then the way the number is factorised is unique.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is to think that "unique" forbids writing 2 × 3 × 5 in any other sequence. Uniqueness here means uniqueness of the multiset of primes, not the order of the symbols on the page.

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic has many applications, both within mathematics and in other fields. Let us look at some examples in the next few topics.

CHECK: The number 32760 has been written as 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 × 13. If a classmate wrote 13 × 7 × 5 × 3² × 2³ instead, would you accept it as the same prime factorisation? Justify using Theorem 1.1.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Can a power of 4 ever end in 0? Theorem 1.1 answers decisively.

WORKED EXAMPLE — Example 1: Consider the numbers 4ⁿ, where n is a natural number. Check whether there is any value of n for which 4ⁿ ends with the digit zero.

Solution: If the number 4ⁿ, for any n, were to end with the digit zero, then it would be divisible by 5. That is, the prime factorisation of 4ⁿ would contain the prime 5. This is not possible because 4ⁿ = (2)²ⁿ; so the only prime in the factorisation of 4ⁿ is 2. So, the uniqueness of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that there are no other primes in the factorisation of 4ⁿ. So, there is no natural number n for which 4ⁿ ends with the digit zero.

WHY THIS STEP? "Ends in 0" means divisible by 10 = 2 × 5, so 5 must appear in the factorisation.

ERROR ALERT: A misconception is that for large n, 4ⁿ eventually picks up a 5. Multiplication cannot create new primes; 5 never enters a product of copies of 4.

CHECK: Can 25ⁿ ever end in 0? Explain using Theorem 1.1.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1: If 4^n ended with the digit 0, it would be divisible by 10 = 2 x 5, so 5 would appear in the prime factorisation of 4^n. Step 2: But 4^n = (2^2)^n = 2^(2n), so the only prime in the factorisation of 4^n is 2. Step 3: By the uniqueness part of Theorem 1.1, no other prime can appear in the factorisation of 4^n, so 5 is not a factor of 4^n. Conclusion: there is no natural number n for which 4^n ends with the digit zero.
recall_questions.prompt: Using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, show whether there is any natural number n for which 4^n ends with the digit zero.

recall_questions.answer: A positive integer ends with the digit 0 exactly when it is divisible by 10. Since 10 = 2 x 5, being divisible by 10 is the same as being divisible by both 2 and 5. So checking whether 4^n ends in 0 reduces to checking whether its prime factorisation contains both 2 and 5.
recall_questions.prompt: Why does the phrase 'ends with the digit zero' translate to 'divisible by both 2 and 5' in this argument?

recall_questions.answer: 25^n = (5^2)^n = 5^(2n), so the only prime in the factorisation of 25^n is 5. For 25^n to end in 0, it would need 2 as a prime factor (since 10 = 2 x 5). By the uniqueness clause of Theorem 1.1, no prime other than 5 appears in 25^n, so 2 is not a factor. Therefore, 25^n can never end with the digit zero.

important_points: We begin with very important properties of positive integers in Sections 1.2, namely the Euclid's division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way — this important fact is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

Theorem 1.1 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) : Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.
The prime factorisation of a natural number is unique, except for the order of its factors.
the only prime in the factorisation of 4ⁿ is 2.
there is no natural number n for which 4ⁿ ends with the digit zero.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (T1 - definition): 'ends with the digit 0' means 'divisible by 10 = 2 x 5', so 5 would have to appear in the prime factorisation of 8^n. Step 2 (T2 - Theorem 1.1): By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, every positive integer has a unique prime factorisation. Factorising, 8^n = (2^3)^n = 2^(3n), so the only prime in the factorisation of 8^n is 2. Step 3 (T3 - uniqueness argument applied as in Example 1): By the uniqueness part of Theorem 1.1, no other prime, including 5, can appear in the factorisation of 8^n. Conclusion: 8^n never ends in the digit zero.
recall_questions.prompt: Using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, show that 8^n cannot end with the digit zero for any natural number n. Indicate at each step which result from this segment you are using.

recall_questions.answer: Existence alone (T2) only tells us that a composite number can be written as some product of primes, but it does not forbid other products of other primes. Uniqueness forbids that: once we have one prime-power factorisation, no other combination of primes can describe the same number. That is the idea Example 1 (T3) uses to rule out 5 appearing in 4^n, and it is the same idea that will later rule out outsider primes in a^2 during the sqrt(2) proof. So every 'can this happen?' question in the segment reduces to 'does this prime already appear in the unique factorisation?'.
recall_questions.prompt: Why is uniqueness, rather than mere existence, the idea that actually drives every argument in this segment? Answer in three or four sentences.

topics.summary: The prime-factorisation method for HCF converts "find the greatest common divisor" into a mechanical procedure. Factorise each number into prime powers, identify the primes that appear in both, and for each such common prime take the smaller exponent; the product of these smallest common powers is the HCF. For example, 6 = 2¹ × 3¹ and 20 = 2² × 5¹ share only the prime 2, whose smaller power is 2¹, so HCF(6, 20) = 2. Similarly, 96 = 2⁵ × 3 and 404 = 2² × 101 give HCF(96, 404) = 2² = 4. This method is the go-to tool whenever a problem demands the greatest shared unit — the largest square tile that fits a rectangular floor, the biggest bundle size that splits two stocks exactly.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: A Pune school tiles its 468 cm × 396 cm hall with identical squares, no tile cut. The largest side divides both — the HCF of 468 and 396.

RECALL: You have already learnt how to find the HCF and LCM of two positive integers using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic in earlier classes. This method is also called the prime factorisation method. We use a and b for the two integers.

CORE: Factorise each. For each common prime, take the smaller power and multiply.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Example 2: Find the HCF of 6 and 20 by the prime factorisation method.

Solution: We have 6 = 2¹ × 3¹ and 20 = 2 × 2 × 5 = 2² × 5¹. You can find HCF(6, 20) = 2 as done in your earlier classes.

Note that HCF(6, 20) = 2¹ = Product of the smallest power of each common prime factor in the numbers.

WHY THIS STEP? Only primes in both numbers contribute; 2 qualifies.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 (partially faded) — Example 3 HCF: 96 = 2⁵ × 3 and 404 = 2² × 101. Complete it — the smaller of 2⁵ and 2² gives HCF(96, 404) = 2² = 4.

TILING: Prime-factorise 468 and 396; multiply smallest powers of common primes for the tile side.

ERROR ALERT: A misconception is HCF = product of all primes in either factorisation. That is the LCM.

CHECK: Find HCF(12, 18). Which smaller power did you pick?
topics.original_chunk:
You have already learnt how to find the HCF and LCM of two positive integers using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic in earlier classes, without realising it! This method is also called the prime factorisation method. Let us recall this method through an example.

Example 2 : Find the LCM and HCF of 6 and 20 by the prime factorisation method.

Solution : We have :         6 = 2¹ × 3¹ and  20 = 2 × 2 × 5 = 2² × 5¹.

You can find HCF(6, 20) = 2 and LCM(6, 20) = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60, as done in your earlier classes.

Note that HCF(6, 20) = 2¹ = Product of the smallest power of each common prime factor in the numbers.
concept_bullets: Factorise each number into prime powers first — for example, 6 = 2 × 3 and 20 = 2² × 5 before any HCF step.
Only primes appearing in both factorisations contribute to the HCF — for example, 3 is in 6 but not in 20, so 3 does not enter HCF(6, 20).
For each common prime, pick the smaller exponent — for example, 96 = 2⁵ × 3 and 404 = 2² × 101 share 2, smaller power 2², so HCF(96, 404) = 4.
Multiply those smallest powers to get the HCF — for example, HCF(6, 20) = 2¹ = 2, and HCF(468, 396) = 2² × 3² = 36 cm for the Pune hall tile.

For example, 6 = 2¹ × 3¹ and 20 = 2² × 5¹ share only the prime 2, whose smaller power is 2¹, so HCF(6, 20) = 2. Similarly, 96 = 2⁵ × 3 and 404 = 2² × 101 give HCF(96, 404) = 2² = 4. This method is the go-to tool whenever a problem demands the greatest shared unit — the largest square tile that fits a rectangular floor, the biggest bundle size that splits two stocks exactly.

The HCF uses only common primes raised to their smallest power; the LCM uses all primes involved raised to their greatest power. Correct working: 12 = 2^2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3^2. Common primes: 2 and 3. Smallest powers: 2^1 and 3^1. HCF(12, 18) = 2 x 3 = 6.

segments.summary: This segment builds the skill of computing the HCF of two positive integers from their prime factorisations. Starting with Example 2 on HCF(6, 20) = 2, it extracts the rule: the HCF equals the product of the smallest power of each common prime factor. By the end, students can prime-factorise two numbers, scan for shared primes, and pick the smaller exponent from each column to read off the HCF.
important_points: You have already learnt how to find the HCF and LCM of two positive integers using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic in earlier classes, without realising it! This method is also called the prime factorisation method.
You can find HCF(6, 20) = 2 and LCM(6, 20) = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60, as done in your earlier classes.
HCF(6, 20) = 2¹ = Product of the smallest power of each common prime factor in the numbers.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (interpret): the tile side must divide both 468 and 396, and we want the largest such divisor, which is HCF(468, 396). Step 2 (factorise): 468 = 2^2 x 3^2 x 13 and 396 = 2^2 x 3^2 x 11. Step 3 (smallest power of each common prime): for 2, min(2, 2) = 2 so 2^2; for 3, min(2, 2) = 2 so 3^2; 11 and 13 are not common and so are excluded. Step 4 (multiply): HCF(468, 396) = 2^2 x 3^2 = 4 x 9 = 36. Result: the largest tile side is 36 cm.
recall_questions.prompt: A school caretaker in Pune wants the largest identical square tiles that will exactly cover a 468 cm by 396 cm hall floor with no tile cut. Using the method from this segment, find the largest possible side length of each tile.

recall_questions.answer: Any common divisor of a and b can only contain primes that appear in both factorisations, and for each such prime it can use at most the smallest power present - otherwise it would not divide the number with the lower exponent. Conversely, the product of the smallest powers of all common primes does divide both a and b by construction, so it is a common divisor. No larger common divisor can exist because increasing any exponent would break divisibility. Hence this product is the greatest (highest) common divisor.
recall_questions.prompt: Explain why the 'smallest power of each common prime' rule delivers exactly the HCF, and not some smaller common divisor. Answer in three sentences.

topics.summary: The prime-factorisation method for LCM is the dual of the HCF rule. For each prime that appears in either number, take the greatest exponent in any factorisation, and multiply; the product is the LCM. For example, 6 = 2¹ × 3¹ and 20 = 2² × 5¹ between them involve the primes 2, 3 and 5, with greatest powers 2², 3¹ and 5¹, so LCM(6, 20) = 2² × 3¹ × 5¹ = 60. For the Shivaji Park joggers, 4 = 2² and 6 = 2 × 3 give LCM(4, 6) = 2² × 3 = 12 minutes until they next meet at the gate. The LCM is the tool of choice whenever the question is about the smallest shared cycle or the next time two repeating events coincide.

topics.brief_summary: LCM of two positive integers by prime factorisation is the product of the greatest power of each prime involved in either number, so LCM(6, 20) = 2² × 3¹ × 5¹ = 60.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Anjali and her grandfather jog on a circular 600 m track at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. Anjali takes 4 minutes per round; her grandfather takes 6. Starting together at the gate, when will they next be at the gate at the same moment? The meeting time must be a multiple of both 4 and 6, so we need the smallest common multiple — the LCM.

CORE — Rule for LCM by prime factorisation:

LCM(6, 20) = 2² × 3¹ × 5¹ = Product of the greatest power of each prime factor, involved in the numbers.

In words, list every prime that appears in either number, take the greatest power of that prime in any factorisation, and multiply. For 6 = 2¹ × 3¹ and 20 = 2² × 5¹, the primes involved are 2, 3 and 5. The greatest powers are 2², 3¹ and 5¹. Their product is 2² × 3¹ × 5¹ = 60, so LCM(6, 20) = 60.

WORKED EXAMPLE — Shivaji Park joggers: 4 = 2² and 6 = 2 × 3. Greatest powers are 2² and 3¹, giving LCM(4, 6) = 12 minutes.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is that the LCM always equals the product of the two numbers. That overcounts when the numbers share a prime: 6 × 20 = 120 but LCM(6, 20) = 60.

CHECK: Using the rule above, find LCM(8, 12).

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (factorise): 8 = 2^3 and 12 = 2^2 x 3. Step 2 (primes involved in either number): 2 and 3. Step 3 (greatest power of each prime): for 2, max(3, 2) = 3, so 2^3; for 3, max(0, 1) = 1, so 3^1. Step 4 (multiply): LCM(8, 12) = 2^3 x 3 = 24.
recall_questions.prompt: Find LCM(8, 12) using the prime factorisation method. Show the primes involved and the greatest power picked for each.

recall_questions.answer: The HCF must divide both numbers, so it can only include primes that appear in both factorisations, and at most to the smallest power present (otherwise it would not divide the number with the lower exponent). The LCM must be a multiple of both numbers, so it must include every prime from either factorisation, and to a power high enough to cover the larger demand, which is the greatest power. That is why LCM uses the union of primes with max exponents and HCF uses the intersection with min exponents.

topics.summary: For any two positive integers a and b, the identity HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b links the two quantities directly. Rearranging gives LCM(a, b) = (a × b) / HCF(a, b), which saves us a second factorisation hunt whenever the HCF is already known. The method: prime-factorise one or both numbers, compute HCF, then divide the product a × b by that HCF to get the LCM. For Example 3 with 96 = 2⁵ × 3 and 404 = 2² × 101, HCF(96, 404) = 2² = 4, and so LCM(96, 404) = (96 × 404) / 4 = 9696. The identity also gives a quick verification check: if your computed HCF and LCM satisfy HCF × LCM = a × b, both are likely correct. Note that this identity is specific to two numbers — the three-number analogue fails.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: From the example above, HCF(6, 20) × LCM(6, 20) = 2 × 60 = 120 = 6 × 20. Not a coincidence.

CORE — Two-number identity: For any two positive integers a and b,

HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b.

We can use this result to find the LCM of two positive integers, if we have already found the HCF of the two positive integers. Rearranging,

LCM(a, b) = (a × b) / HCF(a, b).

WORKED EXAMPLE — Example 3: Find the HCF of 96 and 404 by the prime factorisation method. Hence, find their LCM.

Solution:
Step 1: The prime factorisation of 96 and 404 gives
96 = 2⁵ × 3, 404 = 2² × 101.

Step 2: Therefore, the HCF of these two integers is 2² = 4.

WHY THIS STEP? The only common prime is 2 and its smaller power is 2².

Step 3: Apply the identity.
LCM(96, 404) = (96 × 404) / HCF(96, 404) = (96 × 404) / 4 = 9696.

WHY THIS STEP? One division delivers the LCM once the HCF is known, saving a second factorisation hunt.

ERROR ALERT: A misconception is to extend this to three numbers and write HCF(a, b, c) × LCM(a, b, c) = a × b × c. That fails in general, as the next topic shows.

CHECK: You are told HCF(306, 657) = 9. Use the identity to find LCM(306, 657).
topics.original_chunk:
From the example above, you might have noticed that HCF(6, 20) × LCM(6, 20) = 6 × 20. In fact, for any two positive integers a and b, HCF (a, b) × LCM (a, b) = a × b. We can use this result to find the LCM of two positive integers, if we have already found the HCF of the two positive integers.

Example 3: Find the HCF of 96 and 404 by the prime factorisation method. Hence, find their LCM.

Solution : The prime factorisation of 96 and 404 gives :

96 = 2⁵ × 3,  404 = 2² × 101

Therefore, the HCF of these two integers is 2² = 4.

Also, LCM (96, 404) = (96 × 404) / HCF(96, 404) = (96 × 404) / 4 = 9696

Once HCF is known, LCM follows by one division — for example, LCM(96, 404) = (96 × 404) / 4 = 9696.
The identity gives a verification: for any pair, HCF × LCM should equal the product of the numbers — for example, HCF(306, 657) × LCM(306, 657) = 306 × 657.
For three numbers the rule HCF × LCM = product fails — for example, Example 4 shows 6 × 72 × 120 ≠ HCF(6, 72, 120) × LCM(6, 72, 120).

segments.detailed_summary: This segment builds the LCM counterpart to the HCF rule and ties the two together via the product identity. T5 derives the LCM rule: for each prime in either number, take the greatest power, and multiply. T6 then shows that for any two positive integers a and b, HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b, and demonstrates the shortcut LCM(a, b) = (a × b) / HCF(a, b) on Example 3 with 96 and 404. By the end of the segment, students can compute either quantity from the other without a second factorisation hunt.
important_points: LCM (6, 20) = 2² × 3¹ × 5¹ = Product of the greatest power of each prime factor, involved in the numbers.
for any two positive integers a and b, HCF (a, b) × LCM (a, b) = a × b.
We can use this result to find the LCM of two positive integers, if we have already found the HCF of the two positive integers.
Therefore, the HCF of these two integers is 2² = 4.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (T5 prime factorisation): 336 = 2^4 x 3 x 7 and 54 = 2 x 3^3. Step 2 (HCF - smallest power of each common prime): for 2, min(4, 1) = 1 so 2^1; for 3, min(1, 3) = 1 so 3^1; 7 is not common. HCF(336, 54) = 2 x 3 = 6. Step 3 (LCM - greatest power of each prime involved, from T5): for 2, max(4, 1) = 4 so 2^4; for 3, max(1, 3) = 3 so 3^3; for 7, max(1, 0) = 1 so 7^1. LCM(336, 54) = 2^4 x 3^3 x 7 = 16 x 27 x 7 = 3024. Step 4 (T6 verify identity): HCF x LCM = 6 x 3024 = 18144; and 336 x 54 = 18144. Since 18144 = 18144, the identity HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) = a x b holds.
recall_questions.prompt: For the pair (336, 54), compute the HCF and the LCM using prime factorisation, then use the identity HCF x LCM = a x b to verify your answer. State which method from this segment you used at each step.

recall_questions.answer: For any prime t appearing in a or b, let its exponents be e1 and e2. In HCF the exponent of t is min(e1, e2), and in LCM it is max(e1, e2). Multiplying HCF and LCM adds those exponents for each prime, giving min(e1, e2) + max(e1, e2) = e1 + e2, which is exactly the total exponent of t in a x b. Doing this for every prime shows HCF x LCM and a x b have identical prime-power factorisations, so they are equal by the uniqueness part of Theorem 1.1.
recall_questions.prompt: Explain in three to four sentences why HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) must equal a x b, using the exponent-bookkeeping idea.

topics.summary: For three positive integers, the HCF and LCM rules carry over prime by prime, but the two-number product identity does not. For each prime, take the smallest power appearing in all three numbers to build the HCF, and take the greatest power appearing in any of the three to build the LCM. In Example 4, 6 = 2 × 3, 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5 give smallest common powers 2¹ and 3¹, so HCF(6, 72, 120) = 2 × 3 = 6, while greatest involved powers 2³, 3² and 5¹ give LCM(6, 72, 120) = 2³ × 3² × 5¹ = 360. The remark to take home: 6 × 72 × 120 = 51840 ≠ 6 × 360 = 2160, so for three numbers the product rule HCF × LCM = a × b × c is not valid. Use the extended rules for any three-number HCF or LCM problem; reserve the product identity for two numbers only.
topics.topic_name: HCF and LCM of Three Numbers
topics.brief_summary: For three numbers, HCF is the product of the smallest common powers and LCM is the product of the greatest involved powers, so HCF(6,72,120) = 6 and LCM(6,72,120) = 360, with HCF × LCM ≠ 6 × 72 × 120.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: In Ahmedabad, 60 kaju katli, 90 motichoor laddoo, 150 soan papdi into Diwali boxes: largest count = HCF(60, 90, 150). Delhi buses every 15, 20, 25 min: next shared departure = LCM(15, 20, 25).

RECALL: Rules extend from two to three numbers, prime by prime.

WORKED EXAMPLE — Example 4: Find the HCF and LCM of 6, 72 and 120, using the prime factorisation method.

Solution: We have
6 = 2 × 3, 72 = 2³ × 3², 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5.

Here, 2¹ and 3¹ are the smallest powers of the common factors 2 and 3, respectively.

So, HCF(6, 72, 120) = 2¹ × 3¹ = 2 × 3 = 6.

2³, 3² and 5¹ are the greatest powers of the prime factors 2, 3 and 5 respectively involved in the three numbers.

So, LCM(6, 72, 120) = 2³ × 3² × 5¹ = 360.

WHY THIS STEP? The LCM must cover each prime's largest demand across all three numbers.

Remark: Notice, 6 × 72 × 120 ≠ HCF(6, 72, 120) × LCM(6, 72, 120). So, the product of three numbers is not equal to the product of their HCF and LCM.

SWEET-BOX (partially faded): 60 = 2² × 3 × 5, 90 = 2 × 3² × 5, 150 = 2 × 3 × 5². Smallest powers 2¹, 3¹, 5¹. Complete to find the box count.

ERROR ALERT: A misconception is HCF × LCM = product for three numbers. Example 4 refutes it.

CHECK: Compute LCM(15, 20, 25). When do the Delhi buses next leave together after 6:00 a.m.?
topics.original_chunk:
Example 4 : Find the HCF and LCM of 6, 72 and 120, using the prime factorisation method.

Solution : We have :

6 = 2 × 3,  72 = 2³ × 3², 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5

Here, 2¹ and 3¹ are the smallest powers of the common factors 2 and 3, respectively.

So,         HCF (6, 72, 120) = 2¹ × 3¹ = 2 × 3 = 6

2³, 3² and 5¹ are the greatest powers of the prime factors 2, 3 and 5 respectively involved in the three numbers.

So,         LCM (6, 72, 120) = 2³ × 3² × 5¹ = 360

Remark : Notice, 6 × 72 × 120 ≠ HCF (6, 72, 120) × LCM (6, 72, 120). So, the product of three numbers is not equal to the product of their HCF and LCM.
concept_bullets: For three-number HCF, take the smallest power of each common prime — for example, with 6, 72, 120, the shared primes are 2 and 3 with smallest powers 2¹ and 3¹, giving HCF = 6.
For three-number LCM, take the greatest power of each prime involved — for example, 2³ (from 72 or 120), 3² (from 72) and 5¹ (from 120), giving LCM = 360.
The two-number identity HCF × LCM = product does not extend to three numbers — for example, 6 × 72 × 120 = 51840 but HCF × LCM = 6 × 360 = 2160.
The same three-number LCM solves timetabling — for example, Delhi buses every 15, 20, 25 min next leave together after LCM(15, 20, 25) = 300 minutes.

For each prime, take the smallest power appearing in all three numbers to build the HCF, and take the greatest power appearing in any of the three to build the LCM. In Example 4, 6 = 2 × 3, 72 = 2³ × 3² and 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5 give smallest common powers 2¹ and 3¹, so HCF(6, 72, 120) = 2 × 3 = 6, while greatest involved powers 2³, 3² and 5¹ give LCM(6, 72, 120) = 2³ × 3² × 5¹ = 360. The remark to take home: 6 × 72 × 120 = 51840 ≠ 6 × 360 = 2160, so for three numbers the product rule HCF × LCM = a × b × c is not valid. Use the extended rules for any three-number HCF or LCM problem; reserve the product identity for two numbers only.
important_points: Here, 2¹ and 3¹ are the smallest powers of the common factors 2 and 3, respectively.
2³, 3² and 5¹ are the greatest powers of the prime factors 2, 3 and 5 respectively involved in the three numbers.
6 × 72 × 120 ≠ HCF (6, 72, 120) × LCM (6, 72, 120). So, the product of three numbers is not equal to the product of their HCF and LCM.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (factorise): 6 = 2 x 3, 72 = 2^3 x 3^2, 120 = 2^3 x 3 x 5. Step 2 (HCF - smallest power of each common prime): for 2, min(1, 3, 3) = 1 so 2^1; for 3, min(1, 2, 1) = 1 so 3^1; 5 is not common, so it is excluded. HCF(6, 72, 120) = 2 x 3 = 6. Step 3 (LCM - greatest power of each prime involved): for 2, max(1, 3, 3) = 3 so 2^3; for 3, max(1, 2, 1) = 2 so 3^2; for 5, max(0, 0, 1) = 1 so 5^1. LCM(6, 72, 120) = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5 = 360.
recall_questions.prompt: Find the HCF and the LCM of 6, 72 and 120 using the prime factorisation method. Show the smallest and greatest powers you picked for each prime.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (product of the three numbers): 6 x 72 x 120 = 51840. Step 2 (product of their HCF and LCM): HCF x LCM = 6 x 360 = 2160. Step 3 (compare): 51840 is not equal to 2160, so 6 x 72 x 120 is not equal to HCF(6, 72, 120) x LCM(6, 72, 120). Conclusion: the two-number rule HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) = a x b does not extend to three numbers.
recall_questions.prompt: Using the values from Example 4, verify whether 6 x 72 x 120 equals HCF(6, 72, 120) x LCM(6, 72, 120). State what this tells you about the two-number product rule.

recall_questions.answer: The claim is false. Using Example 4, HCF(6, 72, 120) = 6 and LCM(6, 72, 120) = 360, so HCF x LCM = 6 x 360 = 2160. However, 6 x 72 x 120 = 51840, which is not equal to 2160. This single counter-example is enough to refute the claim, so the two-number product rule does not extend to three numbers.
recall_questions.prompt: A student claims that for any three positive integers p, q, r, HCF(p, q, r) x LCM(p, q, r) = p x q x r. Using the numbers 6, 72 and 120, decide whether the claim is true or false and justify.

topics.summary: Word problems about simultaneous events or largest identical groups reduce to picking HCF or LCM and applying the prime-factorisation methods. Strategy: if the question asks for the largest identical group or the greatest shared unit, use HCF; if it asks for the next time two repeating events occur together or the smallest shared cycle, use LCM. In the circular-path problem, Sonia takes 18 minutes per round and Ravi takes 12 minutes; since they meet again when time is a common multiple of both, the answer is LCM(18, 12) = 2² × 3² = 36 minutes. The real-world use of this skill extends to bus schedules, traffic lights, gift-box packing and tile-cutting — every situation where multiple repeating cycles must synchronise or a shared quantity must be maximised.
topics.topic_name: Word Problems Using HCF and LCM
topics.brief_summary: In a word problem, reach for HCF when the question is about the largest identical group and for LCM when it is about the next shared return, as in LCM(18, 12) = 36 minutes for Sonia and Ravi.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Many word problems ask "when will two repeating events meet?" or "what is the largest identical group we can make?" The hardest step is not the arithmetic — it is translating the story into HCF or LCM.

STRATEGY: If the question is about the largest identical group or the greatest shared unit, reach for HCF. If it is about the next time two repeating events happen together, or the smallest shared cycle, reach for LCM.

MODELED EXAMPLE — Anjali and grandfather at Shivaji Park (EX2), using the full translation scaffold:

THE PROBLEM (in words): Anjali takes 4 minutes per round of a circular track; her grandfather takes 6 minutes. They start together at the gate. After how many minutes will they both be back at the gate at the same time?

WHAT'S THE SITUATION?: Two joggers circle the same track at steady paces. Each returns to the gate at regular intervals, but those intervals differ. We want the first common return.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?: Anjali's round time a = 4 minutes. Grandfather's round time b = 6 minutes.

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND?: t, the smallest time (in minutes) at which both joggers are simultaneously at the gate.

TRANSLATE TO MATHS: t must be a multiple of a and a multiple of b, and it must be the smallest such positive number. That is the LCM by definition: t = LCM(a, b) = LCM(4, 6).

SOLVE: 4 = 2² and 6 = 2 × 3. Greatest powers: 2² and 3¹. So LCM(4, 6) = 2² × 3 = 12. Hence t = 12 minutes.

CHECK AGAINST THE SITUATION: After 12 minutes, Anjali has completed 12 ÷ 4 = 3 rounds and her grandfather 12 ÷ 6 = 2 rounds. Both integers — both runners are exactly at the gate.

TRANSFER PROBLEM (partially faded): There is a circular path around a sports field. Sonia takes 18 minutes to drive one round of the field, while Ravi takes 12 minutes for the same. Suppose they both start at the same point and at the same time, and go in the same direction. After how many minutes will they meet again at the starting point? Using the same scaffold, the answer is LCM(18, 12). Prime-factorise: 18 = 2 × 3², 12 = 2² × 3. Complete the last step yourself by taking the greatest power of each prime and multiplying.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is to multiply the two times (18 × 12 = 216 minutes) because "both things happen." That overcounts whenever the times share a prime factor; the LCM, not the product, gives the first common return.

CHECK: Two traffic lights change every 45 seconds and 60 seconds respectively, last in sync at 9:00:00. When do they next change together? HCF or LCM, and why?

concept_bullets: "Largest identical group" or "greatest shared unit" signals HCF — for example, the largest square tile for a 468 cm × 396 cm hall is HCF(468, 396).
"Meet again" or "next simultaneous event" signals LCM — for example, Sonia (18 min) and Ravi (12 min) meet at the starting point after LCM(18, 12) = 36 minutes.
Check the answer against the story — for example, after 36 min Sonia has done 36 ÷ 18 = 2 rounds and Ravi 36 ÷ 12 = 3 rounds, both whole, so both are at the start.
Multiplying the two times overcounts when they share a prime — for example, 18 × 12 = 216 but LCM(18, 12) = 36 gives the first common return.

recall_questions.prompt: State the rule of thumb for deciding whether a word problem calls for HCF or LCM.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (strategy): we want the smallest time that is a multiple of both 18 and 12, which is the LCM. Step 2 (factorise): 18 = 2 x 3^2 and 12 = 2^2 x 3. Step 3 (greatest powers): for 2, max(1, 2) = 2 so 2^2; for 3, max(2, 1) = 2 so 3^2. Step 4 (multiply): LCM(18, 12) = 2^2 x 3^2 = 4 x 9 = 36. Result: they next meet at the starting point after 36 minutes.
recall_questions.prompt: Sonia takes 18 minutes and Ravi takes 12 minutes to complete one round of a circular path, both starting together in the same direction. After how many minutes will they next meet at the starting point? Solve using the appropriate tool.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (strategy): we want the next shared change, i.e. the smallest common multiple, so we use LCM. Step 2 (factorise): 45 = 3^2 x 5 and 60 = 2^2 x 3 x 5. Step 3 (greatest powers): 2^2, 3^2, 5^1. Step 4: LCM(45, 60) = 4 x 9 x 5 = 180 seconds = 3 minutes. Step 5 (context): 9:00:00 + 3 minutes = 9:03:00. The lights next change together at 9:03:00.
recall_questions.prompt: Two traffic lights change every 45 seconds and 60 seconds respectively, and were last in sync at 9:00:00. Decide whether you need HCF or LCM, then compute when they next change together.

   (i) 12, 15 and 21    (ii) 17, 23 and 29    (iii) 8, 9 and 25

5. Check whether 6ⁿ can end with the digit 0 for any natural number n.

6. Explain why 7 × 11 × 13 + 13 and 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 + 5 are composite numbers.

ERROR ALERT: A misconception on Q2 is computing HCF and LCM but skipping the verification. Let's work through this step by step together.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (factorise): 26 = 2 x 13 and 91 = 7 x 13. Step 2 (HCF - smallest power of common primes): only 13 is common; smallest power is 13^1. So HCF(26, 91) = 13. Step 3 (LCM - greatest power of each prime involved): 2^1, 7^1, 13^1. LCM(26, 91) = 2 x 7 x 13 = 182. Step 4 (verify): HCF x LCM = 13 x 182 = 2366; and 26 x 91 = 2366. Since 2366 = 2366, the identity holds.
recall_questions.prompt: Find the HCF and LCM of 26 and 91 by the prime factorisation method, and verify that LCM x HCF equals the product of the two numbers.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1: If 6^n ended in 0, it would be divisible by 10 = 2 x 5, so 5 would have to appear in the prime factorisation of 6^n. Step 2: 6 = 2 x 3, so 6^n = 2^n x 3^n. The only primes in the factorisation of 6^n are 2 and 3. Step 3: By the uniqueness part of Theorem 1.1, no other prime can appear, so 5 is not a factor of 6^n. Conclusion: there is no natural number n for which 6^n ends with the digit zero.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (factor 13 out of both terms): 7 x 11 x 13 + 13 = 13(7 x 11 + 1) = 13 x (77 + 1) = 13 x 78. Step 2: 13 x 78 is the product of two integers, both greater than 1. Step 3: By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, a number expressible as a product of integers greater than 1 is composite (it has factors other than 1 and itself). Conclusion: 7 x 11 x 13 + 13 is composite.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (T8 strategy choice): we want the next simultaneous departure, i.e. the smallest common multiple, so we use LCM (not HCF). Step 2 (T7 factorise): 15 = 3 x 5, 20 = 2^2 x 5, 25 = 5^2. Step 3 (T7 greatest powers): for 2, max(0, 2, 0) = 2 so 2^2; for 3, max(1, 0, 0) = 1 so 3^1; for 5, max(1, 1, 2) = 2 so 5^2. Step 4 (multiply): LCM(15, 20, 25) = 4 x 3 x 25 = 300 minutes = 5 hours. Step 5 (context): 6:00 a.m. + 5 hours = 11:00 a.m. The three buses next leave together at 11:00 a.m.
recall_questions.prompt: At the ISBT depot in Delhi, Bus A leaves every 15 minutes, Bus B every 20 minutes, and Bus C every 25 minutes. All three leave together at 6:00 a.m. Using the three-number prime-factorisation method from this segment, find when they next leave together.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (T8 strategy): the problem asks for the largest identical group, so we use HCF (not LCM). Step 2 (T7 factorise): 60 = 2^2 x 3 x 5, 90 = 2 x 3^2 x 5, 150 = 2 x 3 x 5^2. Step 3 (T7 smallest power of each common prime): for 2, min(2, 1, 1) = 1; for 3, min(1, 2, 1) = 1; for 5, min(1, 1, 2) = 1. Step 4 (multiply): HCF(60, 90, 150) = 2 x 3 x 5 = 30. Step 5 (context): 30 boxes can be packed. Each box contains 60 / 30 = 2 kaju katli, 90 / 30 = 3 motichoor laddoo, and 150 / 30 = 5 soan papdi.
recall_questions.prompt: Three traffic lights at a junction change every 45, 60 and 75 seconds respectively and turn green together at 9:00 a.m. Use prime factorisation to find when they will next turn green together.

recall_questions.answer: Student B is correct. The identity HCF(a, b) x LCM(a, b) = a x b from T6 means that once HCF is known, LCM = (a x b) / HCF, so a single multiplication and division suffice. Working: LCM(306, 657) = (306 x 657) / 9 = 201042 / 9 = 22338. A fresh prime-factorisation hunt would also work but would double the effort, so Student A's method is correct but inefficient.

modules.module_name: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and Its Applications
modules.brief_summary: Module 1 develops the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and uses its unique prime factorisation to compute HCF and LCM by the smallest-common-power and greatest-involved-power rules for two and three positive integers.
modules.detailed_summary: This module develops the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and turns it into two working tools for positive integers: computing the HCF and LCM of two or three numbers, and verifying the product identity HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b. Starting from the observation that every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes in a unique way, it introduces the factor-tree and prime-factorisation methods as the everyday interface to the theorem. Segment S1 states Theorem 1.1 and uses its uniqueness clause to argue that 4ⁿ can never end in the digit zero. Segment S2 converts Theorem 1.1 into the HCF rule "product of the smallest power of each common prime factor", while Segment S3 derives the twin LCM rule "product of the greatest power of each prime factor involved" and the two-number identity. Segment S4 extends both rules to three numbers, shows that HCF(a,b,c) × LCM(a,b,c) ≠ a × b × c, and consolidates the toolkit through the Exercise 1.1 word problems on tiling, jogging, and divisibility. The unifying insight throughout is that the prime-power representation of every positive integer, guaranteed by Theorem 1.1, is what makes HCF, LCM and divisibility arguments mechanical. This prepares the ground for Module 2, where the same theorem is used to prove that √2, √3 and √5 are irrational.
important_points: Euclid's division algorithm, as the name suggests, has to do with divisibility of integers.
Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.
HCF(6, 20) = 2¹ = Product of the smallest power of each common prime factor in the numbers.
LCM (6, 20) = 2² × 3¹ × 5¹ = Product of the greatest power of each prime factor, involved in the numbers.
for any two positive integers a and b, HCF (a, b) × LCM (a, b) = a × b.
6 × 72 × 120 ≠ HCF (6, 72, 120) × LCM (6, 72, 120). So, the product of three numbers is not equal to the product of their HCF and LCM.

modules.summary: Module 2 proves, for the first time in the CBSE curriculum, that √2, √3 and √5 are irrational, replacing the Class IX claim with a genuine argument. It builds the machinery in three steps. First, Theorem 1.2 establishes the key lemma: if a prime p divides a², then p also divides a — proved directly from the uniqueness clause of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Second, the √2 irrationality theorem (Theorem 1.3) applies Theorem 1.2 twice inside a proof-by-contradiction, collapsing the assumption that √2 = a/b with coprime a and b. Third, the template is generalised: √3 is proved irrational by substituting p = 3 throughout, and the results are transferred to mixed expressions like 5 − √3 and 3√2, establishing that a rational added to or multiplied with an irrational remains irrational. Exercise 1.2 consolidates both templates — the squaring template (T12, T13) for √p, and the rearrangement template (T14, T15) for mixed forms — through the questions on √5, 3 + 2√5, 1/√2, 7√5 and 6 + √2. The unifying insight across the module is that proof by contradiction, powered by the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, converts claims about irrationality into purely integer-factorisation arguments.

topics.summary: A number s is irrational if it cannot be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. The p/q test is the working definition: if you can exhibit integers p and q with q ≠ 0 that equal the number, it is rational; if no such pair can ever exist, it is irrational. For example, √2, √3, √15, π, −√2/√3 and the non-repeating non-terminating decimal 0.10110111011110… are all irrational, whereas √9 = 3 = 3/1 is rational despite the radical symbol. In this section, the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic will be used to upgrade the Class IX claim that √2 is irrational to a proof, first via the lemma in Theorem 1.2 and then via a proof by contradiction.

topics.modified_chunk:
1.3 Revisiting Irrational Numbers

HOOK: In Class IX, you accepted that √2 and π are irrational without proof. This section supplies the proofs, using Theorem 1.1 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) as the main tool.

RECALL: In Class IX, you studied irrational numbers, saw how the rationals and irrationals together make up the real numbers, and learnt how to locate irrationals on the number line. However, we did not prove that they were irrationals.

CORE — Definition: A number s is called irrational if it cannot be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. In this section we will prove that √2, √3, √5 and, in general, √p is irrational, where p is a prime.

EXAMPLES: Some examples of irrational numbers, with which you are already familiar, are

√2, √3, √15, π, −√2/√3, 0.10110111011110 …, etc.

Each resists the p/q test. The decimal 0.10110111011110 … neither terminates nor repeats, so no fraction p/q can equal it.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is that any number written with the radical symbol is automatically irrational — students sometimes claim √9 is irrational "because of the √ sign." But √9 = 3 = 3/1, which is rational. The radical symbol does not cause irrationality; the absence of a p/q representation does.

BRIDGE: Before we prove that √2 is irrational, we need the following theorem, whose proof is based on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. That is Theorem 1.2, taken up in the next topic.

CHECK: Apply the p/q test. Is √15 rational or irrational? Is √2/√3 rational or irrational? Justify each in one sentence.
topics.original_chunk:
1.3 Revisiting Irrational Numbers

In Class IX, you were introduced to irrational numbers and many of their properties. You studied about their existence and how the rationals and the irrationals together made up the real numbers. You even studied how to locate irrationals on the number line. However, we did not prove that they were irrationals. In this section, we will prove that √2, √3, √5 and, in general, √p is irrational, where p is a prime. One of the theorems, we use in our proof, is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

Recall, a number 's' is called irrational if it cannot be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Some examples of irrational numbers, with which you are already familiar, are :

√2, √3, √15, π, −√2/√3, 0.10110111011110 …, etc.

Before we prove that √2 is irrational, we need the following theorem, whose proof is based on the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
concept_bullets: A number is irrational exactly when no integers p and q (with q ≠ 0) satisfy the number = p/q — for example, no fraction equals √2 or π.
A non-terminating, non-repeating decimal is irrational — for example, 0.10110111011110… cannot be captured by any single p/q.
The radical symbol does not by itself cause irrationality — for example, √9 = 3 = 3/1 is rational, while √15 cannot be written as p/q.
This section will use the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic to prove √2, √3, √5 and, in general, √p irrational for any prime p.
topics.detailed_summary: A number s is irrational if it cannot be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. The p/q test is the working definition: if you can exhibit integers p and q with q ≠ 0 that equal the number, it is rational; if no such pair can ever exist, it is irrational. For example, √2, √3, √15, π, −√2/√3 and the non-repeating non-terminating decimal 0.10110111011110… are all irrational, whereas √9 = 3 = 3/1 is rational despite the radical symbol. In this section, the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic will be used to upgrade the Class IX claim that √2 is irrational to a proof, first via the lemma in Theorem 1.2 and then via a proof by contradiction.
important_points: In this section, we will prove that √2, √3, √5 and, in general, √p is irrational, where p is a prime.

Since no p/q representation exists, sqrt(15) is irrational.

So sqrt(9) satisfies the p/q form and is rational.

topics.summary: Theorem 1.2 is the single lemma that powers every irrationality proof in this chapter: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a, where a is a positive integer. The proof rests entirely on the uniqueness clause of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Write a = p₁p₂…pₙ; then a² = p₁²p₂²…pₙ², so squaring doubles each exponent but introduces no new primes. If p divides a², uniqueness forces p to be one of p₁, p₂, …, pₙ, which means p already appears in a, so p divides a. For instance, with p = 5 and a² = 225, the factorisation 225 = 3² × 5² contains 5, and indeed a = 15 = 3 × 5 is divisible by 5. The lemma is then applied twice in the √2 proof (T12) and twice again for √3 (T13).
topics.topic_name: Key Lemma: If a Prime Divides a², It Divides a
topics.brief_summary: Theorem 1.2 states that if a prime p divides a², then p divides a; the proof follows because squaring doubles every prime exponent in a without introducing new primes.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: One lemma separates us from the √2 proof: whenever a prime divides a perfect square, it must already divide the number that was squared.

THEOREM STATEMENT:
Theorem 1.2: Let p be a prime number. If p divides a², then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.

GIVEN: p is prime; a is a positive integer; p divides a².

TO PROVE: p divides a.

*PROOF STEPS:

(i) Let the prime factorisation of a be
    a = p₁p₂ … pₙ, where p₁, p₂, …, pₙ are primes, not necessarily distinct.
    WHY? Theorem 1.1 guarantees such a factorisation, unique apart from order.

(ii) Therefore,
    a² = (p₁p₂ … pₙ)(p₁p₂ … pₙ) = p₁²p₂² … pₙ².
    WHY? Multiplying a by itself doubles each prime's exponent.

(iii) Now, we are given that p divides a². Therefore, from the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, it follows that p is one of the prime factors of a².
    WHY? Uniqueness in Theorem 1.1 forbids outsider primes in a².

(iv) However, using the uniqueness part of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, we realise that the only prime factors of a² are p₁, p₂, …, pₙ. So p is one of p₁, p₂, …, pₙ.

(v) Now, since a = p₁p₂ … pₙ, p divides a.
    WHY? A prime appearing in a product divides the product.

CONCLUSION: Hence, if a prime p divides a², then p divides a.  □

The proof is based on a technique called "proof by contradiction" for the upcoming √2 result. (This technique is discussed in some detail in Appendix 1.)

* Not from the examination point of view.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is to read Theorem 1.2 as "if p divides a², then p² divides a." It does not. 2 divides 6² = 36 and 2 divides 6, yet 2² = 4 does not divide 6. The theorem gives one power of p in a, not two.

CHECK: Apply Theorem 1.2 with p = 5 and a² = 225. Does 5 divide a = 15?

recall_questions.answer: Let p be a prime number. If p divides a^2, then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.
recall_questions.prompt: State Theorem 1.2, including its hypothesis and conclusion.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (factorise a): By Theorem 1.1, write a = p_1 p_2 ... p_n, where the p_i are primes (not necessarily distinct). Step 2 (square both sides): a^2 = (p_1 p_2 ... p_n)(p_1 p_2 ... p_n) = p_1^2 p_2^2 ... p_n^2. Step 3 (use the hypothesis): We are given that p divides a^2. By Theorem 1.1's uniqueness, the only primes in the factorisation of a^2 are p_1, p_2, ..., p_n, so p must equal one of the p_i. Step 4 (conclude): Since a = p_1 p_2 ... p_n and p is one of these primes, p divides a.
recall_questions.prompt: Prove that if a prime p divides a^2, then p divides a, where a is a positive integer. Show each step and cite the theorem you use.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (check the hypothesis): 225 = 15^2, so a = 15 and a^2 = 225. 225 / 5 = 45, so 5 divides a^2. Step 2 (apply Theorem 1.2): With p = 5, since 5 divides a^2, Theorem 1.2 guarantees that 5 divides a. Step 3 (verify directly): 15 / 5 = 3, so 5 divides 15. Both the theorem and the direct check agree: 5 divides a = 15.
recall_questions.prompt: Apply Theorem 1.2 with p = 5 and a^2 = 225. Does 5 divide a = 15? Verify by direct computation and state what Theorem 1.2 guarantees.

segments.summary: This segment lays the foundation for the irrationality proofs that follow. T10 revisits the Class IX definition — a number s is irrational if it cannot be written as p/q with integers p and q, q ≠ 0 — and classifies examples such as √2, √3, √15, π, −√2/√3 and the non-repeating decimal 0.10110111011110… . T11 proves Theorem 1.2: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a. The proof is a direct consequence of the uniqueness clause in the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic — squaring a doubles every prime's exponent without adding new primes. By the end, students have a working definition of irrationality and the single lemma they need to attack √2 and √3 in the next segment.

recall_questions.answer: The student is wrong. Theorem 1.2 is stated for any positive integer a and any prime p: 'If p divides a^2, then p divides a.' The proof in T11 factorises a generically as p_1 p_2 ... p_n, so it covers every positive integer, not just a = 6. Concrete verification: take p = 7 and a = 14. Then a^2 = 196. 196 / 7 = 28, so 7 divides a^2, and 14 / 7 = 2, so 7 divides a = 14 as Theorem 1.2 predicts. This check, and the generic proof, together confirm the theorem holds for all positive integers.
recall_questions.prompt: A student claims that Theorem 1.2 applies only to a = 6, the example they worked in class, and would fail for other values. Using the definition of irrational (T10) and Theorem 1.2's proof (T11), argue whether the student is correct. Give one concrete verification.

recall_questions.answer: T10 gives the definition: sqrt(2) is irrational iff it cannot be written as p/q with integers p, q and q not 0. To prove this, we will assume the opposite (sqrt(2) = a/b in lowest terms) and try to derive a contradiction. T11 (Theorem 1.2) is the lever that lets us turn '2 divides a^2' into '2 divides a', and similarly for b. Once both a and b share the factor 2, they are not coprime, contradicting the reduced form assumption. So T10 supplies the target and T11 supplies the tool.
recall_questions.prompt: Explain how the p/q definition of irrational (T10) and Theorem 1.2 (T11) together set up the upcoming proof that sqrt(2) is irrational. Answer in three or four sentences.

HOOK: With Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2 in hand, √2 irrational follows by contradiction (Appendix 1).

THEOREM STATEMENT: Theorem 1.3: √2 is irrational.

GIVEN: Real numbers; we use Theorem 1.2 with p = 2.

TO PROVE: √2 cannot be written as p/q with integers p, q and q ≠ 0.

PROOF STEPS (by contradiction):

(i) Let us assume, to the contrary, that √2 is rational. So, we can find integers r and s (≠ 0) such that
    √2 = r/s.

(ii) Suppose r and s have a common factor other than 1. Then, we divide by the common factor to get
    √2 = a/b, where a and b are coprime.

(iii) So, b√2 = a. Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get
    2b² = a². Therefore, 2 divides a².
    WHY THIS STEP? We squared both sides — why is squaring reversible here? Because both sides are non-negative.

(iv) Now, by Theorem 1.2, it follows that 2 divides a.
    WHY? Theorem 1.2 with p = 2.

(v) So, we can write a = 2c for some integer c. Substituting for a, we get
    2b² = 4c², that is, b² = 2c².
    This means that 2 divides b², and so 2 divides b (again using Theorem 1.2 with p = 2).

(vi) Therefore, a and b have at least 2 as a common factor. But this contradicts the fact that a and b have no common factors other than 1.

CONCLUSION: This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that √2 is rational. So, we conclude that √2 is irrational.  □

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is that proof by contradiction is circular reasoning. It is not: we never assume what we want to prove — we assume its negation and show it forces a logical collision, which rules out the negation.

CHECK: In step (iii), we squared both sides of b√2 = a. State in one sentence why squaring is valid here.

topics.summary: Example 6 shows 5 − √3 is irrational by contradiction, using the rearrangement template rather than squaring. Assume 5 − √3 = a/b with a and b coprime integers and b ≠ 0. Then 5 − a/b = √3, and rearranging gives √3 = (5b − a)/b. Because 5, a and b are integers, the right-hand side (5b − a)/b is a ratio of integers with non-zero denominator, hence rational; so √3 would be rational. But Example 5 (T13) has just shown that √3 is irrational, a contradiction. Therefore 5 − √3 is irrational. The insight is that once √p is known irrational, isolating √p on one side of an assumed equation forces a rational value onto it — a collision with the earlier result. This template works for any "rational ± irrational" expression.

topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: With √2 and √3 irrational, what about 5 − √3? This topic proves the sum/difference case.

CORE — Set-up: In Class IX, we mentioned that:

● the sum or difference of a rational and an irrational number is irrational, and

● the product and quotient of a non-zero rational and irrational number is irrational.

We prove some particular cases here. T14 handles the sum/difference case; T15 handles the product case.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 (complete, first of a T14 → T15 fading pair) — Example 6: Show that 5 − √3 is irrational.

Solution (by contradiction):

Step 1: Assume, to the contrary, that 5 − √3 is rational. So we find coprime a and b (b ≠ 0) such that
    5 − √3 = a/b.

Step 2: Therefore, 5 − a/b = √3. Rearranging,
    √3 = 5 − a/b = (5b − a)/b.

WHY THIS STEP? We isolated √3 to test the right-hand side against p/q.

Step 3: Since a and b are integers, 5 − a/b is rational, and so √3 is rational.

Step 4: But this contradicts the fact that √3 is irrational (Example 5, T13).

Step 5: This contradiction has arisen from our incorrect assumption. So 5 − √3 is irrational.

ERROR ALERT: A misconception is that 5 − √3 could still be rational "because 5 is rational." Cognitive conflict: if so, the rearrangement above forces √3 to be rational, contradicting T13. A rational ± an irrational cannot repair the irrationality.

CHECK: Sketch in two lines how you would show 7 + √2 is irrational. Which earlier result replaces "√3 is irrational"?
topics.original_chunk:
In Class IX, we mentioned that :

● the sum or difference of a rational and an irrational number is irrational and

● the product and quotient of a non-zero rational and irrational number is irrational.

We prove some particular cases here.

Example 6 : Show that 5 – √3 is irrational.

Solution : Let us assume, to the contrary, that 5 – √3 is rational.

That is, we can find coprime a and b (b ≠ 0) such that 5 – √3 = a/b.

Therefore, 5 − a/b = √3.

Rearranging this equation, we get √3 = 5 − a/b = (5b − a)/b.

Since a and b are integers, we get 5 − a/b is rational, and so √3 is rational.

But this contradicts the fact that √3 is irrational.

This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that 5 − √3 is rational.

So, we conclude that 5 − √3 is irrational.

The isolated radical must be irrational by a named earlier result — for example, Example 5 (T13) says √3 is irrational, giving the contradiction.
The same template handles any rational ± irrational — for example, to show 7 + √2 irrational, isolate √2 and cite Theorem 1.3.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (assume rational): Suppose sqrt(5) = a/b with coprime integers a, b and b not 0. Step 2 (rearrange and square): b sqrt(5) = a, so 5 b^2 = a^2, giving 5 divides a^2. Step 3 (Theorem 1.2 with p = 5): 5 divides a. Write a = 5c. Step 4 (substitute): 5 b^2 = 25 c^2, so b^2 = 5 c^2. Hence 5 divides b^2. Step 5 (Theorem 1.2 again with p = 5): 5 divides b. Step 6 (contradiction): 5 divides both a and b, contradicting their coprimality. Step 7 (conclude): sqrt(5) is irrational.
recall_questions.prompt: Prove that sqrt(5) is irrational by adapting the sqrt(2) / sqrt(3) template with p = 5.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (assume rational): Suppose 3 + 2 sqrt(5) = a/b with coprime integers a, b and b not 0. Step 2 (isolate sqrt(5)): 2 sqrt(5) = a/b - 3 = (a - 3b)/b, so sqrt(5) = (a - 3b) / (2b). Step 3 (classify): a and b are integers, so a - 3b is an integer and (a - 3b)/(2b) is rational. Hence sqrt(5) is rational. Step 4 (contradiction): This contradicts Q1, which proved sqrt(5) is irrational. Step 5 (conclude): our assumption was wrong, so 3 + 2 sqrt(5) is irrational.

segments.summary: This segment executes the √p irrationality programme in full. T12 proves Theorem 1.3 — √2 is irrational — by contradiction, assuming √2 = a/b with coprime integers, squaring to 2b² = a², and applying Theorem 1.2 with p = 2 twice to force both 2 | a and 2 | b, which contradicts coprimality. T13 reruns the same argument with p = 3 to prove √3 irrational, establishing the template √p irrational for any prime p. T14 and T15 transfer the template to mixed expressions: 5 − √3 (rational ± irrational) and 3√2 (non-zero rational × irrational) are shown irrational by isolating the radical and appealing to Theorems 1.3 or Example 5. T16 consolidates everything in Exercise 1.2 on √5, 3 + 2√5, 1/√2, 7√5 and 6 + √2. Students leave the segment able to convert any rational-vs-irrational question into a two-step proof by contradiction.
segments.brief_summary: Segment S6 proves √2 (Theorem 1.3) and √3 irrational by contradiction and extends the technique to 5 − √3 and 3√2, closing with Exercise 1.2 practice on √5, 3 + 2√5, 1/√2, 7√5 and 6 + √2.
segments.detailed_summary: This segment executes the √p irrationality programme in full. T12 proves Theorem 1.3 — √2 is irrational — by contradiction, assuming √2 = a/b with coprime integers, squaring to 2b² = a², and applying Theorem 1.2 with p = 2 twice to force both 2 | a and 2 | b, which contradicts coprimality. T13 reruns the same argument with p = 3 to prove √3 irrational, establishing the template √p irrational for any prime p. T14 and T15 transfer the template to mixed expressions: 5 − √3 (rational ± irrational) and 3√2 (non-zero rational × irrational) are shown irrational by isolating the radical and appealing to Theorems 1.3 or Example 5. T16 consolidates everything in Exercise 1.2 on √5, 3 + 2√5, 1/√2, 7√5 and 6 + √2. Students leave the segment able to convert any rational-vs-irrational question into a two-step proof by contradiction.
important_points: Theorem 1.3 : √2 is irrational.
Let us assume, to the contrary, that √2 is rational.
So, we can find integers r and s (≠ 0) such that √2 = r/s .
Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get 2b² = a². Therefore, 2 divides a².
This contradiction has arisen because of our incorrect assumption that √2 is rational.
So, we conclude that √2 is irrational.
Example 5 : Prove that √3 is irrational.
Example 6 : Show that 5 – √3 is irrational.
Example 7 : Show that 3√2 is irrational.
Prove that 3 + 2√5 is irrational.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (T14 rearrangement template - assume rational): Suppose 5 + 3 sqrt(2) = a/b with coprime integers a, b and b not 0. Step 2 (isolate the radical, as in T14 and T15): 3 sqrt(2) = a/b - 5 = (a - 5b)/b, so sqrt(2) = (a - 5b) / (3b). Step 3 (classify): a and b are integers, so a - 5b is an integer and (a - 5b)/(3b) is rational, making sqrt(2) rational. Step 4 (cite): This contradicts Theorem 1.3 (T12), which proved sqrt(2) is irrational. Step 5 (conclude): the assumption is wrong, so 5 + 3 sqrt(2) is irrational. The T12/T13 squaring template was not used directly here; instead its conclusion (sqrt(2) is irrational) was cited as a result.
recall_questions.prompt: Using the methods of this segment, prove that 5 + 3 sqrt(2) is irrational. State at each step whether you are using the T12/T13 squaring template or the T14/T15 rearrangement template.

recall_questions.answer: Theorem 1.1 (FTA) guarantees unique prime factorisation. T11 (Theorem 1.2) uses that uniqueness to say that if a prime p divides a^2, it must already appear in the unique factorisation of a. T12 and T13 use Theorem 1.2 (applied to the numerator and denominator in turn) to force coprime a, b to share a common prime factor, which is the contradiction that proves sqrt(2) and sqrt(3) irrational. T14's proof that 5 - sqrt(3) is irrational then cites T13 directly. So removing Theorem 1.1 collapses Theorem 1.2, which collapses every irrationality result in this segment.
recall_questions.prompt: Why does every proof in this segment ultimately depend on Theorem 1.1? Answer in three or four sentences, tracing the chain from FTA to the irrationality of 5 - sqrt(3).

recall_questions.answer: What is missing is the application of Theorem 1.2 with the specific prime p = 7. Simply pointing to the sqrt(2) case is not a proof; each prime requires its own two applications of Theorem 1.2. Correct skeleton: assume sqrt(7) = a/b with coprime integers a, b, b not 0; squaring, b sqrt(7) = a becomes 7 b^2 = a^2, so 7 divides a^2, and by Theorem 1.2 (with p = 7) 7 divides a; writing a = 7c and substituting gives b^2 = 7 c^2, so 7 divides b. This violates coprimality, so sqrt(7) is irrational. The correct rearrangement the student must show is: 7 b^2 = a^2 (after squaring b sqrt(7) = a).
recall_questions.prompt: A student writes: 'To prove sqrt(7) is irrational, I just say it is like sqrt(2), so it is irrational.' Identify what is missing from this justification and show the correct one-line rearrangement that should appear in the student's proof.

modules.brief_summary: Module 2 proves √2 and √3 are irrational by contradiction, using the lemma that a prime dividing a² must divide a, and extends the technique to mixed expressions such as 5 − √3 and 3√2.
modules.detailed_summary: Module 2 proves, for the first time in the CBSE curriculum, that √2, √3 and √5 are irrational, replacing the Class IX claim with a genuine argument. It builds the machinery in three steps. First, Theorem 1.2 establishes the key lemma: if a prime p divides a², then p also divides a — proved directly from the uniqueness clause of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Second, the √2 irrationality theorem (Theorem 1.3) applies Theorem 1.2 twice inside a proof-by-contradiction, collapsing the assumption that √2 = a/b with coprime a and b. Third, the template is generalised: √3 is proved irrational by substituting p = 3 throughout, and the results are transferred to mixed expressions like 5 − √3 and 3√2, establishing that a rational added to or multiplied with an irrational remains irrational. Exercise 1.2 consolidates both templates — the squaring template (T12, T13) for √p, and the rearrangement template (T14, T15) for mixed forms — through the questions on √5, 3 + 2√5, 1/√2, 7√5 and 6 + √2. The unifying insight across the module is that proof by contradiction, powered by the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, converts claims about irrationality into purely integer-factorisation arguments.
important_points: a number 's' is called irrational if it cannot be written in the form p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.
Theorem 1.2 : Let p be a prime number. If p divides a², then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.
Theorem 1.3 : √2 is irrational.
Suppose r and s have a common factor other than 1. Then, we divide by the common factor to get √2 = a/b, where a and b are coprime.
Squaring on both sides and rearranging, we get 2b² = a². Therefore, 2 divides a².
Now, by Theorem 1.2, it follows that 2 divides a.
But this contradicts the fact that a and b have no common factors other than 1.
the sum or difference of a rational and an irrational number is irrational
the product and quotient of a non-zero rational and irrational number is irrational.

modules.summary: Module 3 closes the chapter by consolidating its three central results — Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.2, and the irrationality of √2 and √3 — into a single synthesis, and by extending the two-number HCF-LCM identity to three numbers. The Note to the Reader gives the correct three-number formula LCM(p, q, r) = (p·q·r·HCF(p, q, r)) / (HCF(p, q)·HCF(q, r)·HCF(p, r)) and the dual expression for HCF(p, q, r). It also confirms the observation from Example 4 that HCF(p, q, r) × LCM(p, q, r) ≠ p × q × r in general. The unifying insight is exponent accounting: for two numbers, each prime has just a minimum and a maximum that sum to the total, which is why the two-number product rule works, while for three numbers a middle exponent is ignored by HCF × LCM, which is why the product rule fails. This connects back to Module 1 (HCF, LCM) and Module 2 (irrationality via FTA), and looks ahead to Chapter 2, where polynomials factor by an analogous uniqueness principle.
