topics.modified_chunk:
1.4 Summary

HOOK: You have travelled from "What is a prime factorisation?" to "Why is √2 irrational?" in one chapter.

CORE — You have studied:

1. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

2. If p is a prime and p divides a², then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.

3. To prove that √2, √3 are irrationals.

Point 1 (Theorem 1.1, T2) drove T3–T7. Point 2 is Theorem 1.2 (T11). Point 3 was proved in T12 (√2, Theorem 1.3) and T13 (√3), by contradiction using Theorem 1.2.

EXTENSION — A Note to the Reader: You have seen that HCF (p, q, r) × LCM (p, q, r) ≠ p × q × r, where p, q, r are positive integers (see Example 8). However, the following results hold good for three numbers p, q and r:

LCM (p, q, r) = (p · q · r · HCF(p, q, r)) / (HCF(p, q) · HCF(q, r) · HCF(p, r))

HCF (p, q, r) = (p · q · r · LCM(p, q, r)) / (LCM(p, q) · LCM(q, r) · LCM(p, r))

For two integers, each prime's min and max exponents sum to its total, so HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b. For three, each prime also has a middle exponent, which HCF × LCM omits; hence the rule fails — Example 4 (T7) showed 6 × 72 × 120 ≠ HCF × LCM.

CONNECT: This feeds Chapter 2, where polynomials factor analogously.

CHECK: Given HCF(p, q, r) = 2, HCF(p, q) = 6, HCF(q, r) = 10, HCF(p, r) = 4, compute LCM(p, q, r) using the Note's formula.
topics.original_chunk:
1.4 Summary

In this chapter, you have studied the following points:

1. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic : Every composite number can be expressed (factorised) as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order in which the prime factors occur.

2. If p is a prime and p divides a², then p divides a, where a is a positive integer.

3. To prove that √2, √3 are irrationals.

[A Note to the Reader]

You have seen that :

HCF (p, q, r) × LCM (p, q, r) ≠ p × q × r, where p, q, r are positive integers (see Example 8). However, the following results hold good for three numbers p, q and r :

LCM (p, q, r) = (p · q · r · HCF(p, q, r)) / (HCF(p, q) · HCF(q, r) · HCF(p, r))

HCF (p, q, r) = (p · q · r · LCM(p, q, r)) / (LCM(p, q) · LCM(q, r) · LCM(p, r))
concept_bullets: Theorem 1.1 drove every HCF and LCM result — for example, HCF(6, 20) = 2 and LCM(6, 20) = 60 came from prime factorisations guaranteed unique by Theorem 1.1.
Theorem 1.2 drove the irrationality proofs — for example, it fires twice for √2 and twice for √3, forcing a prime to divide both a and b simultaneously.

The three-number LCM formula needs the triple HCF and all three pair HCFs — for example, given HCF(p, q, r) = 2, HCF(p, q) = 6, HCF(q, r) = 10, HCF(p, r) = 4, LCM(p, q, r) = (p · q · r · 2)/(6 · 10 · 4).
For three numbers HCF × LCM no longer equals the product — for example, Example 4 showed 6 × 72 × 120 = 51840 while HCF × LCM = 6 × 360 = 2160.

The Note to the Reader then extends the two-number HCF-LCM identity to three numbers. The correct formulas are LCM(p, q, r) = (p · q · r · HCF(p, q, r)) / (HCF(p, q) · HCF(q, r) · HCF(p, r)) and HCF(p, q, r) = (p · q · r · LCM(p, q, r)) / (LCM(p, q) · LCM(q, r) · LCM(p, r)). recall_questions.answer: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (Theorem 1.1) guarantees that every positive integer has a unique prime factorisation apart from order. In HCF/LCM work (T4 to T7), this uniqueness lets us read off the HCF as the product of smallest common prime powers and the LCM as the product of greatest involved prime powers without ambiguity. In the irrationality proofs (T12 and T13), the same uniqueness is what powers Theorem 1.2: if p divides a^2, then p must appear in the unique factorisation of a itself. So one theorem, Theorem 1.1, drives both halves of the chapter.
recall_questions.prompt: Explain, in three to four sentences, how the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic underpins both the HCF/LCM computations in T4 to T7 and the irrationality proofs in T12 and T13.

recall_questions.answer: Step 1 (state the formula): LCM(p, q, r) = (p x q x r x HCF(p, q, r)) / (HCF(p, q) x HCF(q, r) x HCF(p, r)). Step 2 (substitute): numerator = 12 x 30 x 20 x 2 = 14400; denominator = 6 x 10 x 4 = 240. Step 3 (divide): LCM(p, q, r) = 14400 / 240 = 60. Result: LCM(12, 30, 20) = 60.
recall_questions.prompt: Given HCF(p, q, r) = 2, HCF(p, q) = 6, HCF(q, r) = 10 and HCF(p, r) = 4, with p = 12, q = 30, r = 20, compute LCM(p, q, r) using the Note-to-the-Reader formula.

recall_questions.answer: For any prime t, let its exponents in p, q, r be e1, e2, e3. The HCF exponent is min(e1, e2, e3), and the LCM exponent is max(e1, e2, e3). So HCF x LCM contributes min + max for that prime, which in the three-number case ignores the middle exponent. But p x q x r contributes e1 + e2 + e3. These two sums agree for two numbers (min + max = e1 + e2) but differ for three numbers unless min, middle and max happen to coincide. That is why Example 4 gives 6 x 72 x 120 = 51840 while HCF x LCM = 6 x 360 = 2160: the middle exponent of 2 (which is 3) and the middle exponent of 3 (which is 1) are both omitted.
recall_questions.prompt: Justify why HCF(p, q, r) x LCM(p, q, r) is not in general equal to p x q x r. Contrast the two-number and three-number cases using the exponent accounting of a single prime.
